objective: Integrating scheduling-related components into the broader project management plan (scope, cost, quality, risk, procurement)
secondaryObjectives: Developing a schedule approach based on a project's unique characteristics, EEFs, and OPAs
Establishing schedule configuration management policies (accessibility, storage, baseline/change control)

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Scheduling Professional (PMI-SP) Examination Content Outline (2012, revision mark 4/20): Schedule Strategy 14%, Planning and Development 31%, Monitoring and Controlling 35%, Closeout 6%, Stakeholder Communications 14%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of PMI's PDF hosted by a consultancy. Relevant text: Monitoring and Controlling Task 3 'Perform schedule analysis and audit ... in order to identify and report project schedule, status, changes, impacts or issues'; Task 5 'Incorporate approved risk mitigation activities into the schedule, by utilizing defined change control processes'; Task 6 'Update the schedule model and document schedule baseline changes, received through formal change-control processes'. The objective wording here is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's clinic-fitout-variance-pmisp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You join as scheduler on a data center migration at Halcyon Logistics, a fictional company. The schedule was built from the move list alone. Procurement, risk and cost plans live in other documents.
handover: The schedule starts moves in week 6; the procurement plan shows network switches with a 14-week lead time.
The risk register lists a freeze on changes during the April financial close.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the commitments, the work items, the risks and issues, the people's support and the milestones.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each status meeting; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

effects.finding: Change freeze 1 to 20 April for the financial close; two systems need vendor engineers available only on weekends.

options.label: Procurement lead times as predecessors, the freeze and weekend constraints from the risk register, and a PMB under change control

then.log: Week 2: the first move weekend arrives with no switches; 40 people stand by and the move is cancelled.
Week 3: finance refuses, then a move inside the freeze is forced through and breaks the close reporting job.
Week 4: three teams edit the shared schedule; dates shift without record and nobody can say whether the project is late.

procPrompt.title: Moves before the switches arrive
procPrompt.context: The schedule moves systems in week 6; switches arrive week 15 at the earliest.

choices.label: Add procurement activities and lead times as predecessors (order switches now, 14 weeks), and re-sequence the moves

effects.log: Moves now follow the switches' delivery.

choices.feedback: A schedule integrates procurement: deliveries are predecessors of the work that needs them.

choices.label: Add a note that switches may be late
choices.feedback: The logic still shows impossible dates.

choices.label: Keep the dates: procurement will expedite
choices.feedback: Expediting can't beat a 14-week manufacturer lead time.

riskPrompt.title: Moves planned during the freeze
riskPrompt.context: Four moves fall inside the financial-close freeze.

choices.label: Apply the freeze as a calendar constraint, schedule vendor-dependent moves on weekends, and add schedule reserve for the risks in the register

effects.log: The schedule respects the freeze and the register.

choices.feedback: Risk responses and constraints belong in the schedule model.

choices.label: Add two weeks of contingency at the end
choices.feedback: It covers some slip but four moves still clash with the freeze.

choices.label: Ask finance to waive the freeze

effects.log: Finance is asked to waive it.

choices.feedback: The freeze protects the financial close; moving systems during it risks the close.

choices.label: Baseline schedule and cost together as the performance measurement baseline, store it under version control, and route changes through change control

effects.log: The PMB is set and controlled.

choices.feedback: Schedule configuration management keeps a controlled baseline aligned with cost.

choices.label: Baseline the schedule only
choices.feedback: Earned value can't be measured against a cost plan that doesn't match.

choices.label: Don't baseline: the schedule will keep changing
choices.feedback: Without a baseline, there is nothing to measure variance against or control changes to.

reflection.question: Write the schedule management note: how the schedule now reflects procurement, risk and cost, and how it is controlled.

parts.label: Integration
parts.criteria: Switch lead times as predecessors; freeze and weekend constraints; reserve from the register.
parts.modelAnswer: Switch orders and their 14-week lead time now drive the moves; the April freeze and weekend vendor windows are calendar constraints; reserve covers the registered risks.

parts.label: Control
parts.criteria: Schedule and cost baselined together as the PMB, versioned, under change control.
parts.modelAnswer: Schedule and cost form one performance measurement baseline, versioned and changed only through change control.

scoring.modelReasoning: A schedule is one component of the project management plan: procurement lead times are predecessors, risk responses and constraints (freezes, resource windows) are calendars and reserves, and the schedule baseline is set with the cost baseline as the performance measurement baseline. Configuration management keeps the baseline versioned and changed only through change control.
